title: Move your body
hookLine: regular movement has solid evidence for lifting mild low mood

cards: A gray afternoon. Nothing is exactly wrong, but everything feels heavy. The couch is right there.
Your phone is right there. Putting on shoes and going outside feels about as possible as climbing a mountain.
Some people say that if you drag yourself out anyway and walk around the block, you come back just a little lighter. Not fixed. Lighter.
For a long time that was just something people said. Now there are careful trials behind it.

teach.b: Researchers have run many trials where people with low mood are assigned to exercise, often walking, jogging, strength training or yoga, and compared with people who aren't.
Pulled together, these trials find that regular movement reliably lifts mild to moderate low mood, with effects that in some reviews look comparable to other common treatments.
Study quality varies and many are small, so reviewers stay careful, but the evidence here is solid. And it doesn't take marathons. Brisk walking a few times a week has shown benefits.

teach.h: THE BEST AMOUNT IS THE ONE YOU DO.
teach.b: More vigorous movement seems to help somewhat more, but the best amount is the one you'll actually do. Easy beats heroic.

teach.h: HEAVY OR LASTING? GET REAL HELP.
teach.b: One caution that matters: if low mood is heavy, lasts for weeks, or comes with thoughts of harming yourself, movement isn't a replacement for real help.
Talk to a doctor or someone you trust, and if you're in danger, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Then the old movers.
Aristotle's students were called the Peripatetics, from the Greek for a covered walkway at their school, and the story grew that he taught while walking.
The Mevlevi, the Sufi order that grew from Rumi's circle, turn in the sema, a ceremony of remembrance. Buddhist monks practice walking meditation. Some pilgrims walk for weeks.
The Danish philosopher Kierkegaard wrote to his niece that he had walked himself into his best thoughts, and knew of no thought so heavy that one couldn't walk away from it.
Your body isn't the vehicle that carries the real you to the practice. Sometimes it is the practice.

how: Many people use a daily walk, run, swim or class to steady their mood; many traditions include moving practices, from walking meditation and pilgrimage to yoga and the Mevlevi turning.

games.q: a gray afternoon, everything feels heavy. what does the evidence suggest?
o: wait on the couch until you feel like moving.
walk around the block, even slowly.
plan a two-hour gym session for next week.
games.why: small, regular movement helps, and the best amount is the one you actually do. you don't need to feel like it first.

practice: Stand up if you can, roll your shoulders back slowly three times, lift your arms overhead and stretch, then let them fall. Walk around the room or in place at an easy pace, feeling each foot land.
If standing isn't possible, move what you can: hands, shoulders, the breath.

wordCard.voice: Peripatetics, Aristotle's walking students, whose name is a reminder that regular movement, even brisk walking, lifts mild low mood.

orig.note: Greek: a walk, or a covered walkway; Aristotle's school took its name from it.

carryVoice: Your line: move. Any kind counts: a brisk walk, dancing in the kitchen, the stairs instead of the elevator. Day three hundred twenty-one, in motion.
